long.vo: There was a time when a score of one-sixty won you an IPL game. Now, two hundred isn't safe. In twenty twenty-six, teams crossed two hundred more than sixty times. So what happened?

scene.sub: 60+ totals of 200 or more in IPL 2026

long.vo: Between twenty oh-eight and twenty twenty-two, only about seven percent of IPL innings crossed two hundred. Since the Impact Player rule arrived in twenty twenty-three, it's nearly thirty percent. That's four times as often.
Twenty twenty-five set a record, with fifty-two totals of two hundred or more. Twenty twenty-six smashed it, with more than sixty, and that was before the playoffs had even finished.

Now compare the very first IPL season with twenty twenty-five. The average innings went from about one forty-five to one seventy-two. The powerplay jumped from seven runs an over to more than nine. Top-order batters went from a strike rate of one-thirty to over one fifty-eight. But here's the surprising part. Batters still got out every nineteen balls, exactly like in twenty oh-eight. They're not batting longer. They're hitting harder.

So why is this happening? First, the Impact Player rule. Teams get an extra batter, so nobody needs to play safe. Second, power. Modern bats and range-hitting training mean mis-hits now clear the rope. Third, the pitches, built for runs. And fourth, a fearless generation. Teenagers are hitting thirty-five-ball hundreds.

items.d: An extra batter means nobody plays safe

long.vo: And the sixes keep coming. Twenty twenty-five had one thousand two hundred and ninety-four sixes, a record. Twenty twenty-six beat it before the playoffs even started.

Which means par has moved. Two hundred is the new one-sixty. And spinners are vanishing: in twenty twenty-six, they bowled one of the smallest shares of overs in IPL history. Captains are hiding them.

scene.sub: In 2026, spinners bowled one of their smallest shares of overs in IPL history.

long.vo: But is it good for the game? Fans love the sixes. Yet in twenty twenty-five, only about one in five matches was close, the second-lowest share ever. More runs, but fewer thrillers.
